title_vi: VPN hoạt động thế nào? Đường hầm, mã hóa và điều nó không làm

source_snapshot.note: Pinned commit/path body independently hashed as Git blob; computed OID matches provider tree OID. Non-empty source was read; no source-image bytes used.

related.reason_vi: Khóa công khai và chứng chỉ là cách hai đầu đường hầm xác thực nhau.
Cookie là cách trang vẫn nhận ra bạn khi địa chỉ đã đổi.
Luật tường lửa kiểu kill-switch chặn gói đi ngoài đường hầm.

claims.evidence: Source read; OpenVPN (doc/openvpn.8.rst and man-sections) at commit 43aee864957280d3fd060d477f90cb977708ddf9, WireGuard wireguard-tools man pages wg.8 and wg-quick.8 at a998407747005ea7e4e0258d96f105c97241e1d3, MDN (proxy servers and tunneling, HTTP cookies) at a1aa79c09717761fc72c20bac94bb9c430ed487a and OWASP cheat sheets (TLS, credential stuffing, zero trust) at f9a631ec47a5fd134bb83b57ce690d7946360cea read from local shallow clones; MDN has no VPN or tunneling glossary page at that commit. Tunnel, observer, VPN-server and website behaviour observed with a self-written loopback model (Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, AES-GCM, throw-away key), run three times; it is not a real VPN protocol. WireGuard's website documentation, the Linux kernel documentation and VPN RFCs were not read; claims about HTTPS hiding content from the VPN server are general knowledge and were not tested.

mobile.evidence: Chromium (Playwright) rendered lesson.md, converted with markdown-it-py, at each width with optional sections open; the figure scale was measured from the rendered image (smallest figure text as drawn, which occurs at 320 px) and every SVG text box was checked against the viewBox. Not learner testing and not GitHub or a real phone.

claims.claim_vi: The source describes a VPN as a technology creating a secure, encrypted connection over a less secure network such as the public internet, acting as a tunnel so that no external party can see the data; four steps (secure tunnel to the VPN server, encrypt the data, mask the IP address so activity appears to come from the VPN server, route traffic through the VPN server); advantages listed as privacy, anonymity, security, encryption, masking the IP address; disadvantages as VPN blocking, slower connections, trust in the provider.
claims.verified_by: Source body read (1389 bytes, sha256 matches the pinned value).

claims.claim_vi: MDN defines tunneling as transmitting private network data and protocol information through a public network by encapsulating the data.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote). Section 'HTTP tunneling' read.

claims.claim_vi: MDN says proxies can make requests appear as if they originated from the proxy's IP address.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote). Section 'Forwarding client information through proxies' read. The lesson applies the same mechanism to a VPN server by analogy and by the model run; MDN's page is about proxies, not VPNs.

claims.claim_vi: MDN lists session management (sign-in status and similar), personalization and tracking as uses of cookies, and says the server uses cookies to tell whether requests come from the same browser or user.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote).

claims.claim_vi: The OpenVPN manual says --redirect-gateway redirects all outgoing IP traffic over the VPN in three steps: a static route for the remote (VPN server) address through the pre-existing default gateway, deletion of the default gateway route, and a new default gateway set to the VPN endpoint.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote). Option --redirect-gateway read.

claims.claim_vi: The OpenVPN manual says it supports a pre-shared secret key (Static Key mode) or public key security (SSL/TLS mode) using client and server certificates, and that it also supports non-encrypted TCP/UDP tunnels.

claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote). Section DESCRIPTION read.

claims.claim_vi: The OpenVPN manual mentions IPv6 connections of dual-stacked clients leaking around IPv4-only VPN services (--block-ipv6), says that for full leak protection extra route/firewall rules must be in place (--persist-tun), and describes --block-outside-dns (Windows) as blocking DNS servers on other adapters to prevent DNS leaks.
claims.verified_by: Read from a local clone of the repository at the pinned commit (git clone --depth 1; HEAD matched git ls-remote). --block-ipv6 and --persist-tun read in vpn-network-options.rst; --block-outside-dns read in man-sections/windows-options.rst at the same commit.

claims.claim_vi: The WireGuard wg(8) manual says AllowedIPs lists the addresses (with CIDR masks) to which outgoing traffic for a peer is directed; each peer section has a PublicKey; wg-quick(8) says a peer with 0.0.0.0/0 in AllowedIPs makes the interface the default gateway.

claims.claim_vi: The wg-quick(8) manual describes an iptables PostUp/PreDown 'kill-switch' rule that drops packets that are not coming out of the tunnel encrypted or not going through the tunnel.

claims.claim_vi: The OWASP TLS cheat sheet says TLS, correctly implemented, gives confidentiality (protection against attackers reading the contents of the traffic) and integrity, for clients connecting to a web application over HTTPS, and that SSL was the original protocol providing encryption for HTTP traffic in the form of HTTPS.

claims.claim_vi: Model, without tunnel: an on-path observer relay saw 39 bytes from the client containing the destination name, the path and the cookie as plain text, and a 27-byte reply; the website logged the client's label address 127.0.0.2.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed.

claims.claim_vi: Model, with tunnel: the client-side observer saw one connection from 127.0.0.2 to the VPN server's address, a 71-byte message going out and a 59-byte message coming back, the reply arriving 1.8 to 2.6 ms after the request across three runs, and found none of the destination name, the path or the cookie in the bytes.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed. Sizes were identical in all three runs; the timing is one measurement per run on this machine and says nothing about a real VPN.

claims.claim_vi: Model: the outer message is the inner message plus 32 bytes (4-byte length, 12-byte nonce, 16-byte GCM tag); a 32-byte longer inner message (39 to 71 bytes) gave a 32-byte longer outer message (71 to 103 bytes), so message size is visible to the observer.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed. The 4+12+16 breakdown comes from the script's own framing code; the total of 32 was measured.

claims.claim_vi: Model: flipping one bit of the outer message in transit made the VPN server's AES-GCM decryption raise InvalidTag; the server forwarded nothing and the website received no request. This is a property of AES-GCM in this model, not a statement about any real VPN protocol.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed.

claims.claim_vi: Model: the VPN server's own log held the client's address (127.0.0.2), the destination name and the payload in plain text; it sent the inner message on from 127.0.0.3, and the website logged 127.0.0.3 as the source while reading the same cookie value (sid-4711) as in the no-tunnel request; an observer between the VPN server and the website read the payload in plain text.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed. The loopback addresses 127.0.0.2 and 127.0.0.3 are labels for 'client address' and 'VPN server address'.

claims.claim_vi: Model: a destination set to bypass the tunnel (route table entry 'direct') reached the website from 127.0.0.2, the client's real (label) address, while the destination set to use the tunnel arrived from 127.0.0.3.
claims.verified_by: No external page reports this output; observed by running my own model script (vpn_model.py, Python 3.13, cryptography 50.0.1, loopback only, random ports above 20000, throw-away AES-GCM key) three times on the authoring machine; the script is kept in the author's scratchpad and is not committed. This is a model of the idea that the route table decides what enters the tunnel; it does not reproduce OpenVPN or WireGuard routing.

claims.claim_vi: An HTTPS connection hides the content from the VPN server too, because the VPN server only sees the encrypted HTTPS bytes.
claims.section: Giới hạn cần nhớ; Xem sâu hơn
claims.verified_by: Author's general knowledge; not checked against a source or tested. The model has no HTTPS layer. The OWASP sheet read says TLS protects the contents against attackers reading the traffic, which supports the direction but does not mention VPN servers.

claims.claim_vi: Not examined: whether any VPN provider keeps logs, real VPN speed or latency, legal aspects, the handshake and key exchange of OpenVPN or WireGuard, packet-level routing, DNS behaviour on a real client, or protocols other than the two documented here.

design_notes_vi: Một hình hai khung: bốn thẻ nối bằng mũi tên theo đường đi của một yêu cầu (thiết bị, người nghe, máy chủ VPN, trang web) cho thấy ai thấy gì, rồi bốn điều cần nhớ. Không dùng ảnh nguồn.
source_deviations: The source says no external party can see the data transferring; the lesson says that holds only for the tunnel leg, while the VPN server sees the destination (and the content unless the site uses HTTPS) and the leg after the VPN server is not covered by the tunnel.

The source treats encryption as part of what a VPN is; the OpenVPN manual says it also supports non-encrypted tunnels, so the lesson treats the tunnel (encapsulation) and its encryption as two separate things.

The source presents 'traffic is routed through the VPN server' as a fixed step; the lesson says routing rules (OpenVPN redirect-gateway, WireGuard AllowedIPs) decide what enters the tunnel and that anything outside them keeps the real address.

The source lists privacy, anonymity, security, encryption and masking the IP address as five separate advantages; the lesson merges them into three observable questions (what the on-path listener sees, which address the site sees, whom the user must trust) and shows that the site still recognises the session through the cookie and the VPN server sees the client address.

The source's disadvantages are stated without evidence; the lesson ties trust in the provider to the model run, cites OWASP for sites treating VPN-associated addresses differently, and makes no claim about speed because the model cannot measure a real VPN.
The source does not mention the unprotected leg after the VPN server, leaks (IPv6, DNS) or kill-switch rules; the lesson adds them from the OpenVPN and WireGuard manuals.
